title: The Potato's Contribution to Population and Urbanization: Evidence from a Historical Experiment
research_question: Did the introduction of a new high-yield, nutritionally superior staple food crop from the Americas to the Old World contribute to the dramatic increases in population and urbanization observed during the 18th and 19th centuries? How much of the post-1700 rise in population growth and urban population shares can be attributed to this nutritional and agricultural productivity shock?
data_description: The unit of observation is country-century (and, for robustness, city-century) covering 132 Old World countries observed at 1000, 1400, 1500, 1600, 1700, 1800, and 1900 AD. Country-level historical population data come from McEvedy and Jones (1978); city populations (cities with more than 20,000 inhabitants) come from Chandler (1987), Bairoch (1988), and Modelski (2003), yielding a sample of 1,143 cities. Land suitability for cultivating potatoes, other Old World staples (wheat, rice), New World staples (maize, sweet potatoes), and overall agricultural suitability are constructed from the FAO Global Agro-Ecological Zones (GAEZ) 2000 database at the 0.5-degree grid-cell level, aggregated to country shares of suitable land. Additional country-level controls include average elevation and ruggedness (Nunn and Puga), distance to ice-free coast, century-level slave exports, Roman Empire history, and indicators for serfdom/slavery from Murdock's Ethnographic Atlas.
institutional_context: Potatoes were domesticated in the Andes thousands of years ago and were unknown in the Old World until after Columbus's 1492 voyage. They were brought to Europe by the Spanish in the late 16th century, first cultivated in the Canary Islands around 1570, and gradually adopted as a staple field crop in continental Europe by the late 17th century, with approximately 1700 marking the broad introduction date. The crop subsequently diffused to Asia (Philippines, Java, China, India) and later to Africa via European mariners and colonial administrators. Potatoes yield roughly three times more calories per acre than Old World cereals like wheat, oats, and barley, contain nearly all essential vitamins and minerals (notably vitamin C), and can be grown on rugged terrain at high elevations and on fallow grain land. The geographic and climatic requirements for potato cultivation vary substantially across regions, creating heterogeneous capacity to benefit from the new crop. This setting coincided with sharp post-1700 acceleration in global population growth and urbanization.
